name: Chang'e 3 and Yutu
short_status: Landed Dec 14, 2013 in Mare Imbrium; Yutu operated 972 days to Jul 31, 2016; lander signals still confirmed Dec 31, 2025
tagline: CNSA · China · Rover · 2013 · The robotic return Success
stats: since any nation had soft-landed on the Moon (Luna 24, 1976)
Yutu operated, then the longest-serving lunar rover ever
driven by Yutu before its drive mechanism froze
lander lifetime, with signals still confirmed in Dec 2025

facts.label: Organisations
facts.value: CNSA (China)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1 December 2013, 17:30 UTC, Long March 3B from Xichang LC-2

facts.label: Lunar orbit insertion
facts.value: 6 December 2013, 09:53 UTC

facts.label: Landing
facts.value: 14 December 2013, 13:11 UTC, northern Mare Imbrium, east of a 450 m crater

facts.label: Historic first
facts.value: First lunar soft landing by any nation since Luna 24 in August 1976; China third country to soft-land

facts.label: Launch mass / lander mass
facts.value: 3,780 kg at launch; lander about 1,200 kg

facts.label: Yutu rover mass
facts.value: 140 kg including 20 kg science payload (some technical references list 120 kg)

facts.label: Yutu deployed
facts.value: 14 December 2013, 20:35 UTC, about 7 hours after touchdown

facts.label: Yutu distance driven
facts.value: 114.8 m before mobility loss

facts.label: Yutu mobility lost
facts.value: Mechanical control abnormality announced 25 January 2014, near end of second lunar day

facts.label: Yutu end of operations
facts.value: 31 July 2016, after 972 days (design life 3 months); announced 3 August 2016

facts.label: Yutu longevity record
facts.value: Surpassed Lunokhod 1's 322 days; world's longest-serving lunar rover until Yutu 2

facts.label: LUT telescope
facts.value: 150 mm F/3.75 Ritchey-Chretien, 245-345 nm near-UV, limiting magnitude 13; first long-term lunar-surface astronomical observatory

facts.label: Rover radar
facts.value: Ground-penetrating radar: 60 MHz channel to below 100 m, 500 MHz channel to below 30 m

facts.label: Key science result
facts.value: New ilmenite-rich basalt type unlike Apollo or Luna samples; radar showed layered young volcanic terrane, magma activity to about 3 billion years ago

facts.label: Site name
facts.value: Guang Han Gong (Moon Palace), IAU-approved, 154 m diameter feature; nearby craters Zi Wei, Tian Shi, Tai Wei; announced 5 January 2016

facts.label: Status at 7 years (Sep 2020)
facts.value: Lander operational, LUT reported still working by its manager Jing Wang (NAOC); powered by solar panels plus radioisotope heater unit

facts.label: Radio confirmation 2024
facts.value: X-band carrier at 8470 MHz observed 28 February 2024, switching on after lunar sunrise and locking to a Chinese ground station (DF2MZ)

facts.label: Radio confirmation 2025
facts.value: AMSAT-DL reported the lander still transmitting on 31 December 2025, twelve years after landing

timeline: Launch at 17:30 UTC on Long March 3B from Xichang
Soft landing in northern Mare Imbrium at 13:11 UTC, first by anyone since 1976
Yutu rolls onto the surface at 20:35 UTC
NASA's LRO images lander and rover from orbit (NAC M1142582775R)
Yutu mobility failure announced after 114.8 m of driving; instruments keep working
Yutu passes Lunokhod 1 to become the longest-operating lunar rover
New ilmenite-rich basalt type from Yutu data published in Nature Communications
IAU-approved landing site name Guang Han Gong announced
Yutu ceases operating after 972 days, about 10x its 3-month design life
Lander confirmed still operating at 7 years; LUT telescope reported working
DF2MZ logs the lander's 8470 MHz X-band carrier locking to a ground station
AMSAT-DL reports the lander still transmitting, 12 years after landing
